after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 & -6 \\ -15 & 14 & -9 \\ -5 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & a & 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & b & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that $D={P}^{-1}AP$ is a diagonalization of the matrix $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=1\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=2.$

The second column of $P$ corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-\lambda I,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 & -6 \\ -15 & 14 & -9 \\ -5 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 & 8 & -6 \\ -15 & 12 & -9 \\ -5 & 4 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-10 & 8 & -6 & 0 \\ -15 & 12 & -9 & 0 \\ -5 & 4 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 & -3 & 0 \\ -15 & 12 & -9 & 0 \\ -10 & 8 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}(-4{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}).
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}(-4{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}) \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Comparing this with the second column of $P,$ we deduce that ${x}_{2}=0.$ Now, setting ${x}_{3}=5$ and substituting our values for ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ into the general solution, we obtain the following: 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=-\frac{3}{5}.$

content.worked_solution:
Notice that $D={P}^{-1}AP$ is a diagonalization of the matrix $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=1\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=2.$

The third column of $P$ corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-\lambda I,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -7 & 5 \\ 16 & -12 & 10 \\ 8 & -7 & 7\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -7 & 5 \\ 16 & -14 & 10 \\ 8 & -7 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -7 & 5 & 0 \\ 16 & -14 & 10 & 0 \\ 8 & -7 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}8 & -7 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{8}(7{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}).
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}(7{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}) \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Comparing this with the third column of $P,$ we deduce that ${x}_{3}=0.$ Now, setting ${x}_{2}=8$ and substituting our values for ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ into the general solution, we obtain the following: 

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{7}{8}.$

a
D=[−10001000−1]
b

A is not diagonalizable

decision.explanation: A is triangular, so its eigenvalues are -1 (multiplicity 2) and 1. For eigenvalue -1, (A+I)x=0 gives -3x₁+2x₂=0 and x₁-2x₂=0, forcing x₁=x₂=0 while x₃ is free. Thus its eigenspace has dimension 1, less than its algebraic multiplicity 2, so A is not diagonalizable.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

If the matrix $A$ above is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
Since the matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries of the main diagonal. Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{1}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-1}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-(-1)I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). This implies that we will have $3-2=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-1})=1.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is *not* diagonalizable, since 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})+\text{dim}({V}_{-1})=1+1=2\ne 3.\,\times 
$$

content.worked_solution:
Since the matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries of the main diagonal. Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{1}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-1}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-(-1)I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). This implies that we will have $3-2=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-1})=1.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is *not* diagonalizable, since 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})+\text{dim}({V}_{-1})=1+1=2\ne 3.\,\times 
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is (1-λ)(-3-λ)^2. For λ=-3, A+3I has rows (4,0,2), (-2,0,-1), and (0,0,0), so its rank is 1 and its eigenspace has dimension 2. after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

If the matrix $A$ above is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & -3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((-3-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )) & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +3)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{1}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-3}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-(-3)I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ So,

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-3})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})+\text{dim}({V}_{-3})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

Finally, a corresponding diagonal matrix is 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

If the matrix $A$ above is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & -3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((-3-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )) & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +3)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{1}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-3}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-(-3)I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ So,

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-3})=2.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable, since

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{1})+\text{dim}({V}_{-3})=1+2=3.\,✓
$$

Finally, a corresponding diagonal matrix is 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$
